segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we saw that we can use the present tense to refer to the future.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, if we have some future context, we can just use the present tense by itself, so we could say...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I am having breakfast with them tomorrow." Now, in Spanish, you don't say "with them", you say "with they", "with they". So, how would that be first?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And to have breakfast we said was to "unfast", desayunar, like in English, breakfast, break-fast. So, "I'm having breakfast with them tomorrow"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Desayuno con ellos mañana. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And if we don't have a future context, like mañana or any other context is showing us it's the future, we can also use "I am going" to speak about the future. So, you can say "I am going to have breakfast with them." How is that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a desayunar con ellos... con ellos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a desayunar con ellos. Good. And if we had the future context, it doesn't mean we have to say desayuno con ellos mañana, we could also say voy a desayunar con ellos mañana. The fact that we have future context doesn't mean we can't use voy anymore.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we've seen in that way we can use the present to talk about the future. But this doesn't mean that we don't have a future tense in Spanish. We do. Luckily, we don't have to learn any new sounds to master the future tense in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The future tense in Spanish is connected with the past tense that we learned of haber, haber. This past of "I have had breakfast" or "I have eaten", "I have gone". So, let's make a recap of the forms of haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, it's very irregular haber, and we said that a nice trick to remember the different forms of haber is just looking at the two vowel sounds inside the verb haber. So, what are those two vowel sounds?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Let's start with e. What does he mean by itself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I have", spelled h-e. And what other person is connected with "I"? What's the plural of "I", let's say?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "We". So we have he for "I have" and hemos for "we have". What is ha by itself, h-a?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He, sh- he, she, it, or you formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, give me the other two versions now.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Or you, yeah. And has, which is you informal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, that's all set. Let's practice a little bit some structures with haber, just to recap. So, what was "to sleep"? "Dormant"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say "I have slept"? Begin with "I have".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "to recommend"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say "they have recommended it"? "They have recommended it". And I remind you that with these structures with haber, the "it" has to come before haber, there's no option of where to put it. So, "they have recommended it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So these forms that we have, these forms of haber that we have, he, hemos, ha, has, han, are also the endings that we have for the future tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So like I said, we will learn the future tense now without having to learn any new sounds. Now, the interesting thing about the future tense...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...is that we take the verb in its "to" form, whether it's an -ar verb, -er verb, or -ir verb, doesn't matter, and we put the ending at the end of the "to" form and we stress the ending. We are effectively pushing the accent into the future.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, we have comer, and what was "I have" from haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He. So, that's the sound without the h, just the sound: -e. That's the sound that we need for future, for "I".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We add that onto comer, and we get comeré. And that's "I will eat".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, we are pushing the accent into the future, which might just seem like a coincidence, but you can notice that it happens in other languages as well, this phenomenon. For example, in Greek, part of the past tense is to pull the accent back one syllable, to pull the accent back into the past. And actually, this is so important in Greek, that if there is not a syllable there to do it, you add one to pull the accent back into the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is a phenomenon that you see in in different languages, the accents representing somehow or reflecting somehow the concept of of time and tenses.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So here we are pushing the accent into the future: comeré, "I will eat".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You can give me the rest of the versions for the future of comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They or you guys will eat. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to go"? We said it was very irregular. We have voy and vamos and va, but the verb "to go" doesn't look anything like them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ir. Ir in the future is regular. So, we can follow these rules and get the the future tenses of "to go": "I will go", "he will go". So, what is "I will go"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Irán. Like the country. "They will go to Iran."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if we wanted to make it the question: "Will you go?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What was "to find" or "to encounter"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo encontraré. "We will find it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That was an interesting error, because I said "we", so I made "I" plural with "we", and your mind made the "it" plural, ah?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo encontraremos. "He" or "she" or "you formal will find it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo encontrará. "He will find them", or "she will find them", or "you formal will find them"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you made both of them "them" or "they".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we said "he will find them", or "she will find them".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los encontrará. So you want to think about the two things separately, ah? The who is doing the verb and who are they doing it to, who or what are they doing it to.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that quedar means to remain, quedar, and to get the meaning of "I stay", we say "I remain myself". How was that? "I remain myself".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I will stay", then? "I will remain myself".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, but quedaré means "I will remain", and if you want the meaning of "stay", you must must use...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. Me quedaré. "I will remain myself" or "I will stay". "I will stay here"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, it's very important to think out the whole verb, preparar, and then add on the -e: prepararé. Because a very common mistake that that learners make is to say preparé and they miss out the last -ar because they don't think out the whole verb first. So we must think out the whole verb first: preparar, and then add on the ending: prepararé. What was "to wait" or "to hope"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Organizará. So, the useful thing about the accent being on this ending is that we don't have to worry about where the accent goes when we're pronouncing the whole verb. Organizará on the end. Organizará. "They will organize"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cansado. So, how would you say "I will be tired"? "I will be tired".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would "it will be" be from ser? "It will be", using ser.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, very simple the future tense. Doesn't matter if we have -ar, -er, or -ir verb, we are adding on these endings and these endings are the same as the different versions of haber. So if you forget them, we can look back to haber and then we just add that on the end. But in saying that, the future tense is not so often used in Spanish. Most of the time you will find yourself using present or voy a, vamos a, but the future tense does exist and now you know it.
